records.claim: The measurements were not stable because the receiver switched from lock-in mode to hold-over mode rapidly due to the low signal power.

From the tabulated results in Table 2, the mean difference of 1 PPS for the first-hour lock-in mode showed $0.00378~\mu \mathrm{s}$ after changing the mode of hold-over and a shift of $0.225\rightarrow 0.767~\mu \mathrm{s}$ in the 1PPS measurements for the first $5\mathrm{min}$ .

From the tabulated results in Table 2, the mean difference of 1 PPS for the first-hour lock-in mode showed $0.00378~\mu \mathrm{s}$ after changing the mode of hold-over and a shift of $0.225\rightarrow 0.767~\mu \mathrm{s}$ in the 1PPS measurements for the first $5\mathrm{min}$ .

records.claim: For few developed receivers, internal clock system has synchronized RecT with external PPS before operating like TtP = 0, so the receiver delay is not related with TtP.

records.claim: Most commercial receivers do not manage TtP, meaning RecT synchronizes with 10MHz reference firstly and steers to PPS input secondly, causing RecT to correspond to change through TtP changing.
records.quote: However, most of the commercial receivers do not manage TtP, which means RecT synchronizes with $10\mathrm{MHz}$ reference firstly and steers to PPS input secondly. Consequently, RecT will correspond to change through TtP changing, shown as Figure 10b.

records.claim: In the case of continuous operation, RecT is monotone changing as TtP variation, which does not adjust clock-bias after successful positioning.
records.quote: In the case of continuous operation, RecT is monotone changing as TtP variation, which does not adjust clock-bias after successful positioning.

records.claim: In the case of on-off operation, once the clock-bias exceeds adjustment threshold, the restarted receiver has to adjust clock-bias over again, which will keep RecT with the previous cycle of 10MHz phase until clock-bias less than adjustment threshold, making RecT periodic changing as TtP changing.
records.quote: In the case of on-off operation, once the clock-bias exceeds adjustment threshold, the restarted receiver has to adjust clock-bias over again, which will keep RecT with the previous cycle of $10\mathrm{MHz}$ phase until clock-bias less than adjustment threshold. Thus RecT is periodic changing as TtP changing.

records.claim: The change of RecT will directly affect the measurement pseudorange from the receiver, which impacts on calibration result of channel delay.
records.quote: Whichever continuous operation or on-off operation, the change of RecT will directly affect the measurement pseudorange from the receiver, which impacts on calibration result of channel delay.

records.claim: The receiver delay commonly refers to the time bias from radio frequency (RF) signal input to measurement data output.
records.quote: The receiver delay commonly refers to the time bias from radio frequency (RF) signal input to measurement data output.

records.claim: For the timing receiver, the timing receiver delay can be defined as the time bias from RF signal input to PPS output.
records.quote: For the timing receiver, there is also PPS output which always synchronizes with the measurement data, in other words, the timing receiver delay can be defined as the time bias from RF signal input to PPS output [10,19].

records.claim: GNSS receiver delay is divided into two parts: the channel delay existing in pseudorange and the PPS output delay caused by hardware link.
records.quote: Therefore, we divide GNSS receiver delay into two parts as shown in Figure 2. One is the channel delay existing in pseudorange, the other is PPS output delay caused by hardware link.

records.claim: EVM can be equivalently useful as signal to noise ratio and bit error rate
records.quote: We also compare among the different performance metrics and show that EVM can be equivalently useful as signal to noise ratio and bit error rate.

records.claim: EVM expresses the difference between the expected complex voltage of a demodulated symbol and the value of the actual received symbol.
records.quote: EVM expresses the difference between the expected complex voltage of a demodulated symbol and the value of the actual received symbol.

records.claim: Compared to BER, EVM is more of a measure of errors between the measured symbols and expected symbols.
records.quote: Compared to the bit error rate (BER), which gives a simple one-to-one binary decision as to whether a bit is erroneous or not, EVM is more of a measure of errors between the measured symbols and expected symbols.

records.claim: For BER measurement, the signal must be demodulated first at the receiver side.
records.quote: However, for BER measurement, it is incumbent that signal must be demodulated first at the receiver side.

records.claim: For adaptive systems like MBER based adaptive modulation systems, every update in the adaptive algorithm requires feedback from the receiver end for BER measurement.
records.scope_ref: minimum bit error rate (MBER) based adaptive modulation systems
records.quote: For many of today's adaptive systems, viz. minimum bit error rate (MBER) based adaptive modulation systems etc., this means that for every update in the adaptive algorithm, it has to receive feedback from the receiver end

records.claim: EVM can give the desired performance metric before the demodulation can actually takes place.
records.quote: In this paper, we show that for such systems, it is not always necessary to gather feedback from received end; rather EVM can give the desired performance metric before the demodulation can actually takes place.

records.claim: BER is a direct consequence of EVM.
records.quote: This can be done without any major change of algorithm in adaptive systems, since BER is a direct consequence of EVM.

records.claim: BER can be shown as a direct function of the EVM.
records.quote: The novelty in this paper lies in that the BER can be shown as a direct function of the EVM and as such in order to find equivalent performance metric, EVM can be often more useful.

records.claim: Pilots and training bits are always BPSK modulated.

contributions: propose a communication-efficient pre-training framework, DEPT
decouples embeddings from the transformer body while simultaneously training the latter on multiple data sources without requiring a shared vocabulary
train robustly and effectively under significant data heterogeneity
minimize token embedding parameters to only what the data source vocabulary requires, while cutting communication costs
enhance transformer body plasticity and generalization, improving both average perplexity and downstream task performance
enable training with custom optimized vocabularies per data source

records.claim: Magneto is a framework that combines SLMs and LLMs to derive cost-effective and general schema matching solutions.

records.claim: Magneto is structured in two phases: candidate retrieval selects a subset of the possible matches; and reranker, which ranks the candidates to make it easier for users to examine and select matches.

records.claim: Magneto leverages LLMs to automate SLMs fine-tuning by using LLMs to derive data, adding syntactic diversity and capturing different representations for column names and their values, instead of relying on manually created training data and structure-based augmentation.

Using LLMs, we can add syntactic diversity and capture different representations for column names and their values.

records.claim: Magneto addresses the challenge of high costs by using cheaper SLM-based methods for finding candidates, thereby reducing the number of matches that need to be checked by more costly LLM-based rerankers.

records.claim: Magneto variants strike a balance across runtime and accuracy dimensions and have the advantage of requiring no training data, whereas traditional methods tend to cluster at relatively high accuracy with long runtimes or relatively low runtimes with reduced accuracy.

In an active learning loop, we further add to 𝐒 a small number of posts labeled by an oracle (annotation effort) under the target-domain definition from a large unlabeled target-domain dataset 𝐓 . We use a sentence encoder to project the textual posts from 𝐒 and unlabeled query 𝐐 to the same embedding space. We use a cosine similarity metric to select the class-balanced shots most similar to 𝐐 . The text of the selected shots, their labels, and the labeling definitions (corresponding to the original labeling dimension) are used to fill in an instruction template 𝐩 , and finally passed to the pre-trained LM to make a prediction based on the conditional token probability for each class. The novelty of our method stems from: 1) populating the support set 𝐒 with a mixture of source and target domain posts, and 2) communicating the original labeling definitions as part of an instruction template 𝐩 to allow the model to relate the two.

Comparison between transfer and no-transfer scenarios across the target domain annotation sizes split by positive (#MeToo “Sexually Explicit”) and negative (#MeToo “Toxicity”) transfer scenarios. We can see that in the positive transfer scenario, the gain from transfer occurs at ever annotation size, but seem optimal with as few as 100 annotated target samples after which id diminishes.

Impact of target domain annotation size on the proportion of target examples selected as shots for few-shot prompts. We can see that this proportion increases as target domain examples are more likely to be picked as shot by semantic similarity metric.
